entries.bca3b8d29cd1e05e4bdf616cb3c3ea3a3b45fd36: <div sID="gen32501" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="2Tim.2" sID="2Tim.2"/> <div eID="gen32501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32502" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32503" type="x-p"/> In this chapter our apostle gives Timothy many exhortations and directions, which may be of great use to other, both ministers and Christians, for whom they were designed as well as for him. I. He encourages him in his work, showing him whence he must fetch help, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. He must take care of a succession in the ministry, that the office might not die with him, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.2">ver. 2</reference>. III. He exhorts him to constancy and perseverance in this work, as a soldier and as a husbandman, considering what would be the end of all his sufferings, &c., <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.3-2Tim.2.15">ver. 3-15</reference>. IV. He must shun profane and vain babblings (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.16-2Tim.2.18">ver. 16-18</reference>), for they will be pernicious and mischievous. V. He speaks of the foundation of God, which standeth sure, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19-2Tim.2.21">ver. 19-21</reference>. VI. What he is to avoid—youthful lusts, and foolish and unlearned questions; and what to do, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.22-2Tim.2.26">ver. 22, to the end</reference>.
entries.8a71b9777ee287ccf4de9e72729997fa5c9c906c: <div eID="gen32503" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32502" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Ministerial Fortitude. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32504" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Thou therefore, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ. 4 No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of <hi type="italic">this</hi> life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier. <hi type="super">5</hi> And if a man also strive for masteries, <hi type="italic">yet</hi> is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully. <hi type="super">6</hi> The husbandman that laboureth must be first partaker of the fruits. 7 Consider what I say; and the Lord give thee understanding in all things. <div eID="gen32504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32505" type="x-p"/> Here Paul encourages Timothy to constancy and perseverance in his work: <hi type="italic">Be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.1">v. 1</reference>. Observe, Those who have work to do for God must stir up themselves to do it, and strengthen themselves for it. Being strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus may be understood in opposition to the weakness of grace. Where there is the truth of grace there must be a labouring after the strength of grace. As our trials increase, we have need to grow stronger and stronger in that which is good; our faith stronger, our resolution stronger, our love to God and Christ stronger. Or it may be understood in opposition to our being strong in our own strength: "Be strong, not confiding in thy own sufficiency, but in the grace that is in Jesus Christ." Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.6.10">Eph. vi. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">Be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might.</hi> When Peter promised rather to die for Christ than to deny him he was strong in his own strength; had he been strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus, he would have kept his standing better. Observe, 1. There is grace in Christ Jesus; for the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="John.1.17">John i. 17</reference>. There is grace enough in him for all of us. 2. We must be strong in this grace; not in ourselves, in our own strength, or in the grace we have already received, but in the grace that is in him, and that is the way to be strong in grace. 3. As a father exhorts his son, so does Paul exhort Timothy, with great tenderness and affection: <hi type="italic">Thou, therefore, my son, be strong,</hi> &c. Observe, <div eID="gen32505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32506" type="x-p"/> I. Timothy must count upon sufferings, even unto blood, and therefore he must train up others to succeed him in the ministry of the gospel, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.2">v. 2</reference>. He must instruct others, and train them up for the ministry, and so commit to them the things which he had heard; and he must also ordain them to the ministry, lodge the gospel as a trust in their hands, and so commit to them the things which he had heard. Two things he must have an eye to in ordaining ministers:—Their fidelity or integrity ("Commit them to <hi type="italic">faithful men,</hi> who will sincerely aim at the glory of God, the honour of Christ, the welfare of souls, and the advancement of the kingdom of the Redeemer among men"), and also their ministerial ability. They must not only be knowing themselves, but be able to teach others also, and be apt to teach. Here we have, 1. The things Timothy was to commit to others—what he had heard of the apostle among many witnesses; he must not deliver any thing besides, and what Paul delivered to him and others he had received of the Lord Jesus Christ. 2. He was to commit them as a trust, as a sacred deposit, which they were to keep, and to transmit pure and uncorrupt unto others. 3. Those to whom he was to commit these things must be faithful, that is, trusty men, and who were skilful to teach others. 4. Though men were both faithful and able to teach others, yet these things must be committed to them by Timothy, a minister, a man in office; for none must intrude themselves into the ministry, but must have these things committed to them by those already in that office. <div eID="gen32506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32507" type="x-p"/> II. He must <hi type="italic">endure hardness</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou therefore,</hi> &c. 1. All Christians, but especially ministers, <hi type="italic">are soldiers of Jesus Christ;</hi> they fight under his banner, in his cause, and against his enemies, for he is the captain of our salvation, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.10">Heb. ii. 10</reference>. 2. The soldiers of Jesus Christ must approve themselves good soldiers, faithful to their captain, resolute in his cause, and must not give over fighting till <hi type="italic">they are made more than conquerors, through him that loved them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.37">Rom. viii. 37</reference>. 3. Those who would approve themselves good soldiers of Jesus Christ must endure hardness; that is, we must expect it and count upon it in this world, must endure and accustom ourselves to it, and bear it patiently when it comes, and not be moved by it from our integrity. <div eID="gen32507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32508" type="x-p"/> III. He must not entangle himself in the affairs of this world, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.4">v. 4</reference>. A soldier, when he has enlisted, leaves his calling, and all the business of it, that he may attend his captain's orders. If we have given up ourselves to be Christ's soldiers, we must sit loose to this world; and though there is no remedy, but we must employ ourselves in the affairs of this life while we are here (we have something to do here), we must not entangle ourselves with those affairs, so as by them to be diverted and drawn aside from our duty to God and the great concerns of our Christianity. Those who will war the good warfare must sit loose to this world. <hi type="italic">That we may please him who hath chosen us to be soldiers.</hi> Observe, 1. The great care of a soldier should be to please his general; so the great care of a Christian should be to please Christ, to approve ourselves to him. The way to please him who hath chosen us to be soldiers is not to entangle ourselves with the affairs of this life, but to be free from such entanglements as would hinder us in our holy warfare. <div eID="gen32508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32509" type="x-p"/> IV. He must see to it that in carrying on the spiritual warfare he went by rule, that he observed the laws of war (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">If a man strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully.</hi> We are striving for mastery, to get the mastery of our lusts and corruptions, to excel in that which is good, but we cannot expect the prize unless we observe the laws. In doing that which is good we must take care that we do it in a right manner, that our good may not be evil spoken of. Observe here, 1. A Christian is to strive for masteries; he must aim at mastering his own lusts and corruptions. 2. Yet he must strive according to the laws given to him; he must strive lawfully. 3. Those who do so shall be crowned at last, after a complete victory is obtained. <div eID="gen32509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32510" type="x-p"/> V. He must be willing to wait for a recompence (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The husbandman that laboureth must be first partaker of the fruits.</hi> Or, as it should be read, <hi type="italic">The husbandman labouring first must partake of the fruits,</hi> as appears by comparing it with <reference osisRef="Jas.5.7">Jam. v. 7</reference>. If we would be partakers of the fruits, we must labour; if we would gain the prize, we must run the race. And, further, we must first labour as the husbandman does, with diligence and patience, before we are partakers of the fruit; we must do the will of God, before we receive the promises, for which reason we have need of patience, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.36">Heb. x. 36</reference>. <div eID="gen32510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32511" type="x-p"/> The apostle further commends what he had said to the attention of Timothy, and expresses his desire and hope respecting him: <hi type="italic">Consider what I say, and the Lord give thee understanding in all things,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.7">v. 7</reference>. Here, 1. Paul exhorts Timothy to consider those thing about which he admonished him. Timothy must be reminded to use his considering faculties about the things of God. Consideration is as necessary to a good conversation as to a sound conversion. 2. He prays for him: <hi type="italic">The Lord give thee understanding in all things.</hi> Observe, It is God who gives understanding. The most intelligent man needs more and more of this gift. If he who gave the revelation in the word does not give the understanding in the heart, we are nothing. Together with our prayers for others, that the Lord would give them understanding in all things, we must exhort and stir them up to consider what we say, for consideration is the way to understand, remember, and practise, what we hear or read.
entries.cfe479c843d90d3c0363f6bc23e27092720e1926: <div eID="gen32511" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ministerial Encouragements. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32512" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Remember that Jesus Christ of the seed of David was raised from the dead according to my gospel: <hi type="super">9</hi> Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound. <hi type="super">10</hi> Therefore I endure all things for the elect's sakes, that they may also obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory. 11 <hi type="italic">It is</hi> a faithful saying: For if we be dead with <hi type="italic">him,</hi> we shall also live with <hi type="italic">him:</hi> <hi type="super">12</hi> If we suffer, we shall also reign with <hi type="italic">him:</hi> if we deny <hi type="italic">him,</hi> he also will deny us: <hi type="super">13</hi> If we believe not, <hi type="italic">yet</hi> he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself. <div eID="gen32512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32513" type="x-p"/> I. To encourage Timothy in suffering, the apostle puts him in mind of the resurrection of Christ (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Remember that Jesus Christ, of the seed of David, was raised from the dead, according to my gospel.</hi> This is the great proof of his divine mission, and therefore a great confirmation of the truth of the Christian religion; and the consideration of it should make us faithful to our Christian profession, and should particularly encourage us in suffering for it. Let suffering saints remember this. Observe, 1. We are to look to Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith, who, for the joy that was set before him, endured the cross, despised the shame, and has now sat down at the right hand of the throne of God, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">Heb. xii. 2</reference>. 2. The incarnation and resurrection of Jesus Christ, heartily believed and rightly considered, will support a Christian under all sufferings in the present life. <div eID="gen32513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32514" type="x-p"/> II. Another thing to encourage him in suffering was that he had Paul for an example. Observe, <div eID="gen32514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32515" type="x-p"/> 1. How the apostle suffered (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wherein I suffer as an evil-doer;</hi> and let not Timothy the son expect any better treatment than Paul the father. Paul was a man who did good, and yet suffered as an evil-doer: we must not think it strange if those who do well fare ill in this world, and if the best of men meet with the worst of treatment; but this was his comfort <hi type="italic">that the word of God was not bound.</hi> Persecuting powers may silence ministers and restrain them, but they cannot hinder the operation of the word of God upon men's hearts and consciences; that cannot be bound by any human force. This might encourage Timothy not to be afraid of bonds for the testimony of Jesus; for the word of Christ, which ought to be dearer to him than liberty, or life itself, should in the issue suffer nothing by those bonds. Here we see, (1.) The good apostle's treatment in the world: <hi type="italic">I suffer trouble;</hi> to this he was called and appointed. (2.) The pretence and colour under which he suffered: <hi type="italic">I suffer as an evil-doer;</hi> so the Jews said to Pilate concerning Christ, <hi type="italic">If he were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up to thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.18.30">John xviii. 30</reference>. (3.) The real and true cause of his suffering trouble as an evil-doer: <hi type="italic">Wherein;</hi> that is, in or for the sake of the gospel. The apostle suffered trouble unto bonds, and afterwards he resisted unto blood, striving against sin, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.4">Heb. xii. 4</reference>. Though the preachers of the word are often bound, yet the word is never bound. <div eID="gen32515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32516" type="x-p"/> 2. Why he suffered cheerfully: <hi type="italic">I endure all things for the elects' sake,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.10">v. 10</reference>. Observe, (1.) Good ministers may and should encourage themselves in the hardest services and the hardest sufferings, with this, that God will certainly bring good to his church, and benefit to his elect, out of them.—<hi type="italic">That they may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus.</hi> Next to the salvation of our own souls we should be willing to do and suffer any thing to promote the salvation of the souls of others. (2.) The elect are designed to obtain salvation: <hi type="italic">God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.9">1 Thess. v. 9</reference>. (3.) This salvation is in Christ Jesus, in him as the fountain, the purchaser, and the giver of it; and it is accompanied with eternal glory: there is no salvation in Christ Jesus without it. (4.) The sufferings of our apostle were for the elects' sake, for their confirmation and encouragement. <div eID="gen32516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32517" type="x-p"/> III. Another thing with which he encourages Timothy is the prospect of a future state. <div eID="gen32517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32518" type="x-p"/> 1. Those who faithfully adhere to Christ and to his truths and ways, whatever it cost them, will certainly have the advantage of it in another world: <hi type="italic">If we be dead with him, we shall live with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.11">v. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">If we be dead with him, we shall live with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.11">v. 11</reference>. If, in conformity to Christ, we be dead to this world, its pleasures, profits, and honours, we shall go to live with him in a better world, to be for ever with him. Nay, though we be called out to suffer for him, we shall not lose by that. <hi type="italic">Those who suffer for Christ</hi> on earth shall reign with Christ in heaven, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.12">v. 12</reference>. Those who suffered with David in his humiliation were preferred with him in his exaltation: so it will be with those who suffer with the Son of David. <div eID="gen32518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32519" type="x-p"/> 2. It is at our peril if we prove unfaithful to him: <hi type="italic">If we deny him, he also will deny us.</hi> If we deny him before man, he will deny us before his Father, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.33">Matt. x. 33</reference>. And that man must needs be for ever miserable whom Christ disowns at last. This will certainly be the issue, whether we believe it or no (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful; he cannot deny himself.</hi> He is faithful to his threatenings, faithful to his promises; neither one nor the other shall fall to the ground, no, not the least, jot nor tittle of them. If we be faithful to Christ, he will certainly be faithful to us. If we be false to him, he will be faithful to his threatenings: <hi type="italic">he cannot deny himself,</hi> cannot recede from any word that he hath spoken, for he is yea, and amen, the faithful witness. Observe, (1.) Our being dead with Christ precedes our living with him, and is connected with it: the one is in order to the other; so our suffering for him is the way to reign with him. <hi type="italic">You that have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of man shall sit on the throne of his glory, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Matt. xix. 28</reference>. (2.) This is a faithful saying, and may be depended on and ought to be believed. But, (3.) If we deny him, out of fear, or shame, or for the sake of some temporal advantage, he will deny and disown us, and will not deny himself, but will continue faithful to his word when he threatens as well as when he promises.
entries.0348f22dfdc3f1a91f8ba03cdcf2f05ce59e92c3: <div eID="gen32519" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Cautions against Error. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32520" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Of these things put <hi type="italic">them</hi> in remembrance, charging <hi type="italic">them</hi> before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, <hi type="italic">but</hi> to the subverting of the hearers. <hi type="super">15</hi> Study to show thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. <hi type="super">16</hi> But shun profane <hi type="italic">and</hi> vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness. <hi type="super">17</hi> And their word will eat as doth a canker: of whom is Hymenæus and Philetus; <hi type="super">18</hi> Who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already; and overthrow the faith of some. <div eID="gen32520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32521" type="x-p"/> Having thus encouraged Timothy to suffer, he comes in the next place to direct him in his work. <div eID="gen32521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32522" type="x-p"/> I. He must make it his business to edify those who were under his charge, <hi type="italic">to put them in remembrance</hi> of those things which they did already know; for this is the work of ministers; not to tell people that which they never knew before, but to put them in mind of that which they do know, <hi type="italic">charging them that they strive not about words.</hi> Observe, Those that are disposed to strive commonly strive about matters of very small moment. Strifes of words are very destructive to the things of God. That they strive not about words <hi type="italic">to no profit.</hi> If people did but consider of what little use most of the controversies in religion are, they would not be so zealous in their strifes of words, <hi type="italic">to the subverting of the hearers,</hi> to the drawing of them away from the great things of God, and occasioning unchristian heats and animosities, by which truth is often in danger of being lost. Observe, People are very prone to strive about words, and such strifes never answer any other ends than to shake some and subvert others; they are not only useless, but they are very hurtful, and therefore ministers are to charge the people that they do not strive about words, and they are most likely to be regarded when they charge them before the Lord, that is, in his name and from his word; when they produce their warrant for what they say.—<hi type="italic">Study to show thyself approved unto God,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.15">v. 15</reference>. Observe, The care of ministers must be to approve themselves unto God, to be accepted of him, and to show that they are so approved unto God. In order thereunto, there must be constant care and industry: <hi type="italic">Study to show thyself</hi> such a one, <hi type="italic">a workman that needs not be ashamed.</hi> Ministers must be workmen; they have work to do, and they must take pains in it. Workmen that are unskilful, or unfaithful, or lazy, have need to be ashamed; but those who mind their business, and keep to their work, are workmen that need not be ashamed. And what is their work? It is <hi type="italic">rightly to divide the word of truth.</hi> Not to invent a new gospel, but rightly to divide the gospel that is committed to their trust. To speak terror to those to whom terror belongs, comfort to whom comfort; to give every one <hi type="italic">his portion in due season,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.45">Matt. xxiv. 45</reference>. Observe here, 1. The word which ministers preach is the word of truth, for the author of it is the God of truth. 2. It requires great wisdom, study, and care, to divide this word of truth rightly; Timothy must study in order to do this well. <div eID="gen32522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32523" type="x-p"/> II. He must take heed of that which would be a hindrance to him in his work, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.16">v. 16</reference>. He must take heed of error: <hi type="italic">Shun profane and vain babblings.</hi> The heretics, who boasted of their notions and their arguments, thought their performances such as might recommend them; but the apostle calls them <hi type="italic">profane and vain babblings:</hi> when once men become fond of those <hi type="italic">they will increase unto more ungodliness.</hi> The way of error is down-hill; one absurdity being granted or contended for, a thousand follow: <hi type="italic">Their word will eat as doth a canker, or gangrene;</hi> when errors or heresies come into the church, the infecting of one often proves the infecting of many, or the infecting of the same person with one error often proves the infecting of him with many errors. Upon this occasion the apostle mentions some who had lately advanced erroneous doctrines: <hi type="italic">Hymeneus and Philetus.</hi> He names these corrupt teachers, by which he sets a brand upon them, to their perpetual infamy, and warns all people against hearkening to them. They have <hi type="italic">erred concerning the truth,</hi> or concerning one of the fundamental articles of the Christian religion, which is truth. The resurrection of the dead is one of the great doctrines of Christ. Now see the subtlety of the serpent and the serpent's seed. They did not deny the resurrection (for that had been boldly and avowedly to confront the word of Christ), but they put a corrupt interpretation upon that true doctrine, saying that the resurrection was past already, that what Christ spoke concerning the resurrection was <hi type="italic">to be understood mystically</hi> and by way of allegory, that it must be meant of a spiritual resurrection only. It is true, there is a spiritual resurrection, but to infer thence that there will not be a true and real resurrection of the body at the last day is to dash one truth of Christ in pieces against another. By this they <hi type="italic">overthrew the faith of some,</hi> took them off from the belief of the resurrection of the dead; and if there be no resurrection of the dead, nor future state, no recompence of our services and sufferings in another world, we are of men the most miserable, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.19">1 Cor. xv. 19</reference>. Whatever takes away the doctrine of a future state overthrows the faith of Christians. The apostle had largely disproved this error (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.1-1Cor.15.58">1 Cor. xv.</reference>), and therefore does not here enter into the arguments against it. Observe, 1. The babblings Timothy was to shun were profane and vain; they were empty shadows, and led to profaneness: <hi type="italic">For they will increase unto more ungodliness.</hi> 2. Error is very productive, and on that account the more dangerous: it <hi type="italic">will eat like a gangrene.</hi> 3. When men err concerning the truth, they always endeavour to have some plausible pretence for it. Hymeneus and Philetus did not deny a resurrection, but pretended it was already past. 4. Error, especially that which affects the foundation, will overthrow the faith of some.
entries.a25d29daf4d93e685e5e63c15a37dc47ba292037: <div eID="gen32523" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Cautions against Error. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32524" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity. 20 But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of earth; and some to honour, and some to dishonour. <hi type="super">21</hi> If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, <hi type="italic">and</hi> prepared unto every good work. <div eID="gen32524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32525" type="x-p"/> Here we see what we may comfort ourselves with, in reference to this, and the little errors and heresies that both infect and infest the church, and do mischief. <div eID="gen32525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32526" type="x-p"/> I. It may be a great comfort to us that the unbelief of men cannot make the promise of God of no effect. Though the faith of some particular persons be overthrown, yet <hi type="italic">the foundation of God standeth sure</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">v. 19</reference>); it is not possible that they should deceive the elect. Or it may be meant of the truth itself, which they impugn. All the attacks which the powers of darkness have made upon the doctrine of Christ cannot shake it; it stands firm, and weathers all the storms which have been raised against it. The prophets and apostles, that is, the doctrines of the Old and New Testament, are still firm; and they have a seal with two mottoes upon it, one on the one side, and the other on the other, as is usual in a broad seal. 1. One expresses our comfort—that <hi type="italic">the Lord knows those that are his,</hi> and those that are not; knows them, that is, he owns them, so knows them that he will never lose them. Though the faith of some be overthrown, yet the Lord is said to know the ways of the righteous, <reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Ps. i. 6</reference>. None can overthrow the faith of any whom God hath chosen. 2. Another declares our duty—that every one who names the name of Christ must depart from iniquity. Those who would have the comfort of the privilege must make conscience of the duty. If the name of Christ be called upon us, we must depart from iniquity, else he will not own us; he will say in the great day (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.23">Matt. vii. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">Depart from me, I never knew you, you workers of iniquity.</hi> Observe, (1.) Whatever errors are introduced into the church, the foundation of God standeth sure, his purpose can never be defeated. (2.) God hath some in the church who are his and whom he knows to be his. (3.) Professing Christians name the name of Christ, are called by his name, and therefore are bound to depart from iniquity; for Christ <hi type="italic">gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.2.14">Tit. ii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen32526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32527" type="x-p"/> II. Another thing that may comfort us is that though there are some whose faith is overthrown, yet there are others who keep their integrity, and hold it fast (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">In a great house there are not only vessels of gold,</hi> &c. The church of Christ is a great house, a well-furnished house: now some of the furniture of this house is of great value, as the plate in a house; some of small value, and put to mean uses, as the vessels of wood and earth; so it is in the church of God. There are some professors of religion that are like the vessels of wood and earth, they are vessels of dishonour. But at the same time all are not vessels of dishonour; there are <hi type="italic">vessels of gold and silver,</hi> vessels of honour, <hi type="italic">that are sanctified and meet for the Master's use.</hi> When we are discouraged by the badness of some, we must encourage ourselves by the consideration of the goodness of others. Now we should see to it that we be vessels of honour: we must <hi type="italic">purge ourselves from these corrupt opinions,</hi> that we may be sanctified for our Master's use. Observe, 1. In the church there are some vessels of honour and some of dishonour; there are some vessels of mercy and other vessels of wrath, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.22-Rom.9.23">Rom. ix. 22, 23</reference>. Some dishonour the church by their corrupt opinions and wicked lives; and others honour and credit it by their exemplary conversation. 2. A man must purge himself from these before he can be a vessel of honour, or meet for his Master's use. 3. Every vessel must be fit for its Master's use; every one in the church whom God approves must be devoted to his Master's service and meet for his use. 4. Sanctification in the heart is our preparation for every good work. The tree must be made good, and then the fruit will be good.
entries.6f657cc7550106efff6d09c0db3e64fc4d0f25ee: <div eID="gen32527" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Cautions against Contention. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32528" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart. <hi type="super">23</hi> But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all <hi type="italic">men,</hi> apt to teach, patient, <hi type="super">25</hi> In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth; <hi type="super">26</hi> And <hi type="italic">that</hi> they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will. <div eID="gen32528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32529" type="x-p"/> I. Paul here exhorts Timothy to beware of <hi type="italic">youthful lusts,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.22">v. 22</reference>. Though he was a holy good man, very much mortified to the world, yet Paul thought it necessary to caution him against youthful lusts: "<hi type="italic">Flee</hi> them, take all possible care and pains to keep thyself pure from them." The lusts of the flesh are youthful lusts, which young people must carefully watch against, and the best must not be secure. He prescribes an excellent remedy against youthful lusts: <hi type="italic">Follow righteousness, faith, charity peace,</hi> &c. Observe, 1. Youthful lusts are very dangerous, for which reason even hopeful young people should be warned of them, for they war against the soul, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.11">1 Pet. ii. 11</reference>. 2. The exciting of our graces will be the extinguishing of our corruptions; the more we follow that which is good the faster and the further we shall flee from that which is evil. Righteousness, and faith, and love, will be excellent antidotes against youthful lusts. Holy love will cure impure lust.—<hi type="italic">Follow peace with those that call on the Lord.</hi> The keeping up of the communion of saints will take us off from all fellowship with unfruitful works of darkness. See the character of Christians: they are such as <hi type="italic">call on the Lord Jesus Christ, out of a pure heart.</hi> Observe, Christ is to be prayed to. It is the character of all Christians that they call upon him; but our prayers to God and Christ are not acceptable nor successful except they come out of a pure heart. <div eID="gen32529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32530" type="x-p"/> II. He cautions him against contention, and, to prevent this (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.23">v. 23</reference>), cautions him against <hi type="italic">foolish and unlearned questions,</hi> that tend to no benefit, strifes of words. Those who advanced them, and doted upon them, thought themselves wise and learned; but Paul calls them foolish and unlearned. The mischief of these is that they <hi type="italic">gender strifes,</hi> that they breed debates and quarrels among Christians and ministers. It is very remarkable how often, and with what seriousness, the apostle cautions Timothy against disputes in religion, which surely was not without some such design as this, to show that religion consists more in believing and practising what God requires than in subtle disputes.—<hi type="italic">The servant of the Lord must not strive,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24">v. 24</reference>. Nothing worse becomes the servant of the Lord Jesus, who himself did not strive nor cry (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.19">Matt. xii. 19</reference>), but was a pattern of meekness, and mildness, and gentleness to all, than strife and contention. The servant of the Lord must be <hi type="italic">gentle to all men,</hi> and thereby show that he is himself subject to the commanding power of that holy religion which he is employed in preaching and propagating.—<hi type="italic">Apt to teach.</hi> Those are unapt to teach who are apt to strive, and are fierce and froward. Ministers must be patient, bearing with evil, and <hi type="italic">in meekness instructing</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.25">v. 25</reference>) not only those who subject themselves, but those who oppose themselves. Observe, 1. Those who oppose themselves to the truth are to be instructed; for instruction is the scripture-method of dealing with the erroneous, which is more likely to convince them of their errors than fire and faggot: he does not bid us kill their bodies, under pretence of saving their souls. 2. Such as oppose themselves are to be instructed in meekness, for our Lord is meek and lowly (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Matt. xi. 29</reference>), and this agrees well with the character of the servant of the Lord (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">He must not strive, but be gentle to all men, apt to teach, patient.</hi> This is the way to convey truth in its light and power, and to overcome evil with good, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.21">Rom. xii. 21</reference>. 3. That which ministers must have in their eyes, in instructing those who oppose themselves, must be their recovery: <hi type="italic">If God, peradventure, will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth.</hi> Observe, (1.) Repentance is God's gift. (2.) It is a gift with a <hi type="italic">peradventure</hi> in the case of those who oppose themselves; and therefore, though we are not to despair of the grace of God, yet we must take heed of presuming upon it. <hi type="italic">To the acknowledging of the truth.</hi> (3.) The same God who gives us the discovery of the truth does by his grace bring us to the acknowledging of it, otherwise our hearts would continue in rebellion against it, for we are to confess with our mouths as well as to believe with our hearts, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.9-Rom.10.10">Rom. x. 9, 10</reference>. And thus sinners recover themselves out of the snare of the devil; see here, [1.] The misery of sinners: they are in the <hi type="italic">snare of the devil, and are led captive by him at his will,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.26">v. 26</reference>. They are slaves to the worst of task-masters; he is the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Eph. ii. 2</reference>. They are taken in a snare, and in the worst snare, because it is the devil's; they are as fishes that are taken in n evil net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare. Further, They are under Ham's curse (<hi type="italic">a servant of servants shall he be,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.9.25">Gen. ix. 25</reference>), they are slaves to him who is but a slave and vassal. [2.] The happiness of those who repent: they recover themselves out of this snare, as a bird out of the snare of the fowler; the snare is broken and they have escaped; and the greater the danger the greater the deliverance. When sinners repent, those who before were led captive by the devil at his will come to be led into the glorious liberty of the children of God, and have their wills melted into the will of the Lord Jesus. The good Lord recover us all out of the snare.  <chapter eID="2Tim.2"/> <div eID="gen32530" type="x-p"/>

entries.02f4e548c7e3ca86c5c84087b646564f09bd9618: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18186"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <div sID="gen37610" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.1-2Tim.2.26">2Ti 2:1-26</reference>. Exhortations; to Faithfulness as a Good Soldier of Christ; Errors to Be Shunned; the Lord's Sure Foundation; the Right Spirit for a Servant of Christ.<div eID="gen37610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37611" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18186"/><hi type="bold">1. Thou therefore--</hi>following my example (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.8">2Ti 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>), and that of Onesiphorus (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.16-2Tim.1.18">2Ti 1:16-18</reference>), and shunning that of those who forsook me (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.15">2Ti 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen37611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37612" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my son--</hi>Children ought to imitate their father.<div eID="gen37612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37613" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be strong--</hi>literally, "be invested with power." Have power, and show thyself to have it; implying an abiding state of power.<div eID="gen37613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37614" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the grace--</hi>the element IN which the believer's strength has place. Compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.7">2Ti 1:7</reference>, "God hath given us the spirit of power." <div eID="gen37614" type="x-p"/>
entries.c9b8bbc603fcc881574cbaa7c66c2ced55fbda8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18187"/><div sID="gen37615" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18187"/><hi type="bold">2. among--</hi>Greek, "through," that is, with the attestation (literally, "intervention") of many witnesses, namely, the presbyters and others present at his ordination or consecration (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.14">1Ti 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.12">6:12</reference>).<div eID="gen37615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37616" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commit--</hi>in trust, as a deposit (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.14">2Ti 1:14</reference>).<div eID="gen37616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37617" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faithful--</hi>the quality most needed by those having a trust committed to them.<div eID="gen37617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37618" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who--</hi>Greek, "(persons) such as shall be competent to teach (them to) others also." Thus the way is prepared for inculcating the duty of faithful endurance (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.3-2Tim.2.13">2Ti 2:3-13</reference>). Thou shouldest consider as a motive to endurance, that thou hast not only to keep the deposit for thyself, but to transmit it unimpaired to others, who in their turn shall fulfil the same office. This is so far from supporting oral tradition now that it rather teaches how precarious a mode of preserving revealed truth it was, depending, as it did, on the trustworthiness of each individual in the chain of succession; and how thankful we ought to be that God Himself has given the written Word, which is exempt from such risk. <div eID="gen37618" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0c6cc5a582648ecea94df7589a1ca0a993ac96b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18188"/><div sID="gen37619" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18188"/><hi type="bold">3. Thou therefore endure hardness--</hi>The oldest manuscripts have no "Thou therefore," and read, "Endure hardship with (me)." "Take thy share in suffering" [Conybeare and Howson]. <div eID="gen37619" type="x-p"/>
entries.1605b42813512daf80b46cc777d073b6b41e580e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18189"/><div sID="gen37620" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18189"/>4. "No one while serving as a soldier."<div eID="gen37620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37621" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the affairs of (this) life--</hi>"the businesses of life" [Alford]; mercantile, or other than military.<div eID="gen37621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37622" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him who hath chosen him--</hi>the general who at the first enlisted him as a soldier. Paul himself worked at tent-making (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.3">Ac 18:3</reference>). Therefore what is prohibited here is, not all other save religious occupation, but the becoming entangled, or over-engrossed therewith. <div eID="gen37622" type="x-p"/>
entries.77cabab02c11ce44003480a48363b14937991d7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18190"/><div sID="gen37623" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18190"/><hi type="bold">5. And--</hi>"Moreover."<div eID="gen37623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37624" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strive for masteries--</hi>"strive in the games" [Alford]; namely, the great national games of Greece.<div eID="gen37624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yet is he not crowned, except--</hi>even though he gain the victory.<div eID="gen37625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37626" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strive lawfully--</hi>observing all the conditions of both the contest (keeping within the bounds of the course and stript of his clothes) and the preparation for it, namely, as to self-denying diet, anointing, exercise, self-restraint, chastity, decorum, &c. (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.24-1Cor.9.27">1Co 9:24-27</reference>). <div eID="gen37626" type="x-p"/>
entries.cd43f2a2c9b3ddcf68ffa778bc547f3eb823b8c7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18191"/><div sID="gen37627" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18191"/><hi type="bold">6. must be first partaker--</hi>The right of first partaking of the fruits belongs to him who is laboring; do not thou, therefore, relax thy labors, as thou wouldest be foremost in partaking of the reward. Conybeare explains "first," before the idler. <div eID="gen37627" type="x-p"/>
entries.b566c7ba42b202cd561eff33bae725a859a185ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18192"/><div sID="gen37628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18192"/>7. Consider the force of the illustrations I have given from the soldier, the contender in the games, and the husbandmen, as applying to thyself in thy ministry.<div eID="gen37628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the Lord give, &c.--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "for the Lord will give thee understanding." Thou canst understand my meaning so as personally to apply it to thyself; for the Lord will give thee understanding when thou seekest it from Him "in all things." Not intellectual perception, but personal appropriation of the truths metaphorically expressed, was what he needed to be given him by the Lord. <div eID="gen37629" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e0caf36ca1c1fc8d02d069e65689e94a635c71e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18193"/><div sID="gen37630" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18193"/>8. Rather as Greek, "Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead." Remember Christ risen, so as to follow Him. As He was raised after death, so if thou wouldest share His risen "life," thou must now share His "death" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.11">2Ti 2:11</reference>). The Greek perfect passive participle, implies a permanent character acquired by Jesus as the risen Saviour, and our permanent interest in Him as such. Christ's resurrection is put prominently forward as being the truth now assailed (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Ti 2:18</reference>), and the one best calculated to stimulate Timothy to steadfastness in sharing Paul's sufferings for the Gospel's sake (see on <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.3">2Ti 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen37630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37631" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the seed of David--</hi>The one and only genealogy (as contrasted with the "endless genealogies," <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4">1Ti 1:4</reference>) worth thinking of, for it proves Jesus to be the Messiah. The absence of the article in the Greek, and this formula, "of the seed of David" (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.1.3">Ro 1:3</reference>), imply that the words were probably part of a recognized short oral creed. In His death He assured us of His humanity; by His resurrection, of His divinity. That He was not crucified for His own sin appears from His resurrection; that He was crucified shows that He bore sin, on Him, though not in Him.<div eID="gen37631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37632" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my gospel--</hi>that which I always taught. <div eID="gen37632" type="x-p"/>
entries.831c34c78f882bc6c584904319eb3d32f1c90b3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18194"/><div sID="gen37633" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18194"/><hi type="bold">9. Wherein--</hi>in proclaiming which Gospel.<div eID="gen37633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37634" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">suffer trouble--</hi>literally, "evil." I am a sufferer of evil as though I were a doer of evil.<div eID="gen37634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bonds--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.16">2Ti 1:16</reference>).<div eID="gen37635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37636" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">word ... not bound--</hi>Though my person is bound, my tongue and my pen are not (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17">2Ti 4:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.28.31">Ac 28:31</reference>). Or he alludes not merely to his own proclamation of the Gospel, though in chains, but to the freedom of its circulation by others, even though his power of circulating it is now prescribed (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.18">Php 1:18</reference>). He also hints to Timothy that he being free ought to be the more earnest in the service of it. <div eID="gen37636" type="x-p"/>
entries.81fb239f27aae6dd601ae75b980c067473bf0869: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18195"/><div sID="gen37637" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18195"/><hi type="bold">10. Therefore--</hi>Because of the anxiety I feel that the Gospel should be extended; that anxiety being implied in <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.9">2Ti 2:9</reference>.<div eID="gen37637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37638" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">endure--</hi>not merely "I passively suffer," but "I actively and perseveringly endure," and "am ready to endure patiently all things."<div eID="gen37638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37639" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the elect's sakes--</hi>for the sake of the Church: all the members of Christ's spiritual body (<reference osisRef="Col.1.24">Col 1:24</reference>).<div eID="gen37639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37640" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they ... also--</hi>as well as myself: both God's elect not yet converted and those already so.<div eID="gen37640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37641" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">salvation ... glory--</hi>not only salvation from wrath, but glory in reigning with Him eternally (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.12">2Ti 2:12</reference>). Glory is the full expansion of salvation (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.47">Ac 2:47</reference>; Ro 8:21-24, 30; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">He 9:28</reference>). So grace and glory (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.12">Psa 84:12</reference>). <div eID="gen37641" type="x-p"/>
entries.774907a99a5ec8081696f19761083273c074f65d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18196"/><div sID="gen37642" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18196"/>11. Greek, "Faithful is the saying."<div eID="gen37642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">For--</hi>"For" the fact is so that, "if we be dead with Him (the Greek aorist tense implies a state once for all entered into in past times at the moment of regeneration, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.3">Ro 6:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.8">4, 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.12">Col 2:12</reference>), we shall also live with Him." The symmetrical form of "the saying," <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.11-2Tim.2.13">2Ti 2:11-13</reference>, and the rhythmical balance of the parallel clauses, makes it likely, they formed part of a Church hymn (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>), or accepted formula, perhaps first uttered by some of the Christian "prophets" in the public assembly (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.26">1Co 14:26</reference>). The phrase "faithful is the saying," which seems to have been the usual formula (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">1Ti 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">4:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.8">Tit 3:8</reference>) in such cases, favors this. <div eID="gen37643" type="x-p"/>
entries.d4be8b617c96f480940e752de897ae63a7df4cde: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18197"/><div sID="gen37644" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18197"/><hi type="bold">12. suffer--</hi>rather, as the Greek is the same as in <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.10">2Ti 2:10</reference>, "If we endure (with Him)" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.17">Ro 8:17</reference>).<div eID="gen37644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37645" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reign with him--</hi>The peculiar privilege of the elect Church now suffering with Christ, then to reign with Him (see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.2">1Co 6:2</reference>). Reigning is something more than mere salvation (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.17">Ro 5:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Re 3:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.10">5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.4">20:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen37645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37646" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deny--</hi>with the mouth. As "believe" with the heart follows, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.12">2Ti 2:12</reference>. Compare the opposite, "confess with thy mouth" and "believe in thine heart" (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.9">Ro 10:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen37646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37647" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he also will deny us--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.10.33">Mt 10:33</reference>). <div eID="gen37647" type="x-p"/>
entries.387bd7ad0bdbf171d6eebd435385cc13fddc84aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18198"/><div sID="gen37648" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18198"/><hi type="bold">13. believe not--</hi>"If we are unbelievers (literally, 'unfaithful'), He remains faithful" (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.9">De 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.7.10">10</reference>). The oldest manuscripts read, "For He cannot (it is an impossibility that He should) deny Himself." He cannot be unfaithful to His word that He will deny those who deny Him, though we be not faithful to our profession of faith in Him (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.3">Ro 3:3</reference>). Three things are impossible to God, to die, to lie, and to be deceived [Augustine, The Creed, 1.1], (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.18">He 6:18</reference>). This impossibility is not one of infirmity, but of infinite power and majesty. Also, indirectly, comfort is suggested to believers, that He is faithful to His promises to them; at the same time that apostates are shaken out of their self-deceiving fancy, that because they change, Christ similarly may change. A warning to Timothy to be steadfast in the faith. <div eID="gen37648" type="x-p"/>
entries.3756d8193adfa65ccd0726139f00dd96d23413c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18199"/><div sID="gen37649" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18199"/><hi type="bold">14. them--</hi>those over whom thou dost preside (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.1">Tit 3:1</reference>).<div eID="gen37649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37650" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">charging--</hi>Greek, "testifying continually": "adjuring them."<div eID="gen37650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37651" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before the Lord--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.21">1Ti 5:21</reference>).<div eID="gen37651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37652" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they strive not about words--</hi>rather, "strive with words": "not to have a (mere) war of words" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.23">2Ti 2:23</reference>, 24; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.4">1Ti 6:4</reference>) where the most vital matters are at stake (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.17">2Ti 2:17</reference>, 18; <reference osisRef="Acts.18.15">Ac 18:15</reference>). The oldest manuscripts put a stop at "charging them before the Lord" (which clause is thus connected with "put them in remembrance") and read the imperative, "Strive not thou in words," &c.<div eID="gen37652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37653" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to no profit--</hi>not qualifying "words"; but Greek neuter, in apposition with "strive in words," "(a thing tending) to no profit," literally, "profitable for nothing"; the opposite of "meet for the master's use" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.21">2Ti 2:21</reference>).<div eID="gen37653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37654" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the subverting--</hi>sure to subvert (overturn) the hearers: the opposite of "edifying" (building up) (<reference osisRef="2Cor.13.10">2Co 13:10</reference>). <div eID="gen37654" type="x-p"/>
entries.f63d45075debf396090a2b7ccba1008573911269: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18200"/><div sID="gen37655" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18200"/><hi type="bold">15. Study--</hi>Greek, "Be earnest," or "diligent."<div eID="gen37655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37656" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to show--</hi>Greek, "present," as in <reference osisRef="Rom.12.1">Ro 12:1</reference>.<div eID="gen37656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37657" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thyself--</hi>as distinguished from those whom Timothy was to charge (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.14">2Ti 2:14</reference>).<div eID="gen37657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">approved--</hi>tested by trial: opposed to "reprobate" (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.16">Tit 1:16</reference>).<div eID="gen37658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">workman--</hi>alluding to <reference osisRef="Matt.20.1">Mt 20:1</reference>, &c.<div eID="gen37659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37660" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not to be ashamed--</hi>by his work not being "approved" (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.20">Php 1:20</reference>). Contrast "deceitful workers" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.13">2Co 11:13</reference>).<div eID="gen37660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37661" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rightly dividing--</hi>"rightly handling" [Vulgate]; "rightly administering" [Alford]; literally, cutting "straight" or "right": the metaphor being from a father or a steward (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.1">1Co 4:1</reference>) cutting and distributing bread among his children [Vitringa and Calvin], (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.42">Lu 12:42</reference>). The Septuagint, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.6">Pr 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.11.5">11:5</reference>, use it of "making one's way": so Bengel here takes Paul to mean that Timothy may make ready a straight way for "the word of truth," and may himself walk straight forward according to this line, turning neither to the right nor to the left, "teaching no other doctrine" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>). The same image of a way appears in the Greek for "increase" (see on <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.16">2Ti 2:16</reference>). The opposite to "rightly handling," or "dispensing," is, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2Co 2:17</reference>, "corrupt the word of God."<div eID="gen37661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">truth--</hi>Greek, "the truth" (compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Ti 2:18</reference>). <div eID="gen37662" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0c55e550109bec0e0d8963d158a0a0b20af1b9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18201"/><div sID="gen37663" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18201"/><hi type="bold">16. shun--</hi>literally, "stand above," separate from, and superior to.<div eID="gen37663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37664" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vain--</hi>opposed to "the truth" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.15">2Ti 2:15</reference>).<div eID="gen37664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37665" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">babblings--</hi>with loud voice: opposed to the temperate "word" (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.9">Tit 3:9</reference>).<div eID="gen37665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">increase--</hi>Greek, advance"; literally, "strike forward": an image from pioneers cutting away all obstacles before an advancing army. They pretend progress; the only kind of progress they make is to a greater pitch of impiety.<div eID="gen37666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37667" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">more ungodliness--</hi>Greek, "a greater degree of impiety." <div eID="gen37667" type="x-p"/>
entries.8bff8b0663956f1663c62fc43707a653b21ddf43: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18202"/><div sID="gen37668" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18202"/><hi type="bold">17. will eat--</hi>literally, "will have pasture." The consuming progress of mortification is the image. They pretend to give rich spiritual pasture to their disciples: the only pasture is that of a spiritual cancer feeding on their vitals.<div eID="gen37668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37669" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">canker--</hi>a "cancer" or "gangrene."<div eID="gen37669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37670" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hymenaeus--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.20">1Ti 1:20</reference>). After his excommunication he seems to have been readmitted into the Church and again to have troubled it. <div eID="gen37670" type="x-p"/>
entries.6fce202c9eee280144ec3acd14390c4d4328da8c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18203"/><div sID="gen37671" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18203"/><hi type="bold">18. erred--</hi>Greek, "missed the aim" (see <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.21">1Ti 6:21</reference>).<div eID="gen37671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37672" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is past already--</hi>has already taken place. The beginnings of the subsequent Gnostic heresy already existed. They "wrested" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.16">2Pe 3:16</reference>) Paul's own words (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.4">Ro 6:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.6">Ep 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.12">Col 2:12</reference>) "to their own destruction," as though the resurrection was merely the spiritual raising of souls from the death of sin. Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.12">1Co 15:12</reference>, where he shows all our hopes of future glory rest on the literal reality of the resurrection. To believe it past (as the Seleucians or Hermians did, according to Augustine [Epistles, 119.55, To Januarius, 4]), is to deny it in its true sense.<div eID="gen37672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">overthrow--</hi>trying to subvert "the foundation" on which alone faith can rest secure (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Ti 2:19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Titus.1.11">Tit 1:11</reference>). <div eID="gen37673" type="x-p"/>
entries.110ddfef1471b07054d459c64daf803c85ea6e11: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18204"/><div sID="gen37674" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18204"/><hi type="bold">19. Nevertheless--</hi>Notwithstanding the subversion of their faith, "the firm foundation of God standeth" fast (so the Greek ought to be translated). The "foundation" here is "the Church" [Alford], "the ground" or basement support "of the truth" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1Ti 3:15</reference>), Christ Himself being the ultimate "foundation" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">1Co 3:11</reference>). In the steadfast standing of the Church there is involved the steadfast certainty of the doctrine in question (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Ti 2:18</reference>). Thus the "house" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.20">2Ti 2:20</reference>) answers to the "foundation"; it is made up of the elect whom "the Lord knoweth" (acknowledgeth, recognizes, <reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Psa 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.7.23">Mt 7:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.14">Joh 10:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.3">1Co 8:3</reference>) as "His," and who persevere to the end, though others "err concerning the faith" (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.24">Mt 24:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.28">Joh 10:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.38">Ro 8:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.39">39</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.19">1Jo 2:19</reference>). Bengel takes "the foundation" to be the immovable faithfulness of God (to His promises to His elect [Calvin]). This contrasts well with the erring from the faith on the part of the reprobate, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Ti 2:18</reference>. Though they deny the faith, God abates not His faithfulness (compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.13">2Ti 2:13</reference>).<div eID="gen37674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37675" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having--</hi>seeing that it has [Ellicott].<div eID="gen37675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37676" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seal--</hi>"inscription": indicating ownership and destination: inscriptions were often engraven on a "foundation" stone (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.14">Re 21:14</reference>) [Alford]. This will agree with the view that "the foundation" is the Church (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Ep 2:20</reference>). If it be taken God's immovable faithfulness, the "seal" will be regarded as attached to His covenant promise, with the inscription or legend, on one side of its round surface, "The Lord knoweth (it is 'knew' in the Septuagint, <reference osisRef="Num.16.5">Nu 16:5</reference>, to which Paul here alludes, altering it for his purpose by the Spirit) them that are His"; on the observe side, "Let every one that nameth (as his Lord, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference>, or preacheth in His name, <reference osisRef="Jer.20.9">Jr 20:9</reference>) Christ."<div eID="gen37676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">depart--</hi>Greek, "stand aloof."<div eID="gen37677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from iniquity--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.52.11">Is 52:11</reference>). In both clauses there may be an allusion to <reference osisRef="Num.16.5">Nu 16:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.16.26">26</reference>, Septuagint. God's part and man's part are marked out. God chooseth and knoweth His elect; our part is to believe, and by the Spirit depart from all iniquity, an unequivocal proof of our being the Lord's (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.29.29">De 29:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.13.23-Luke.13.27">Lu 13:23-27</reference>). St. Lucian when asked by his persecutors, "Of what country art thou?" replied, "I am a Christian." "What is your occupation? ... I am a Christian." "Of what family? ... I am a Christian." [Chrysostom, Orations, 75]. He cannot be honored with the name Christian, who dishonors by iniquity, Christ, the Author of the name. Blandina's refreshment amidst her tortures was to say, "I am a Christian, and with us Christians no evil is done" [Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, 5.1]. Apostasy from the faith is sure soon to be followed by indulgence in iniquity. It was so with the false teachers (2Ti 3:<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.13">2-8, 13</reference>). <div eID="gen37678" type="x-p"/>
entries.17a9fd5acb35a1bc49bb987e9a532f794d83588b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18205"/><div sID="gen37679" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18205"/><hi type="bold">20. in a great house--</hi>that is, the visible professing Christian Church (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1Ti 3:15</reference>). Paul is speaking, not of those without, but of the [visible] family of God [Calvin]. So the parable of the sweep-net (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.47-Matt.13.49">Mt 13:47-49</reference>) gathering together of every kind, good and bad: as the good and bad cannot be distinguished while under the waves, but only when brought to shore, so believers and unbelievers continue in the same Church, until the judgment makes the everlasting distinction. "The ark of Noah is a type of the Church; as in the former there were together the leopard and the kid, the wolf and the lamb; so in the latter, the righteous and sinners, vessels of gold and silver, with vessels of wood and earth" [Jerome, Dialogue against the Luciferians, 302] (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.20.16">Mt 20:16</reference>).<div eID="gen37679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37680" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vessels of gold ... silver--</hi>precious and able to endure fire.<div eID="gen37680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37681" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of wood and earth--</hi>worthless, fragile, and soon burnt (1Co 3:12-15; 15:<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.47">47</reference>).<div eID="gen37681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37682" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">some ... some--</hi>the former ... the latter.<div eID="gen37682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37683" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to dishonour--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.16.4">Pr 16:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.17-Rom.9.23">Ro 9:17-23</reference>). <div eID="gen37683" type="x-p"/>
entries.119e853032d37ddaeb3015e43efe199f84e00b7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18206"/><div sID="gen37684" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18206"/><hi type="bold">21. If a man ... purge himself from these--</hi>The Greek expresses "If one (for example, thou, Timothy) purify himself (so as to separate) from among these" (vessels unto dishonor).<div eID="gen37684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37685" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sanctified--</hi>set apart as wholly consecrated to the Lord.<div eID="gen37685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37686" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and meet--</hi>Some oldest manuscripts omit "and."<div eID="gen37686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37687" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the master's--</hi>the Lord's. Paul himself was such a vessel: once one among those of earth, but afterwards he became by grace one of gold.<div eID="gen37687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37688" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prepared unto every good work--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.17">2Ti 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.1">Tit 3:1</reference>). Contrast <reference osisRef="Titus.1.16">Tit 1:16</reference>. <div eID="gen37688" type="x-p"/>
entries.c205a05d708a6a7a50805a8cabf1430f1460c0a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18207"/><div sID="gen37689" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18207"/><hi type="bold">22. Flee--</hi>There are many lusts from which our greatest safety is in flight (<reference osisRef="Gen.39.12">Ge 39:12</reference>). Avoid occasions of sin. From the abstemious character of Timothy (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.23">1Ti 5:23</reference>) it is likely that not animal indulgences, but the impetuosity, rash self-confidence, hastiness, strife, and vainglory of young men (<reference osisRef="1John.2.14-1John.2.16">1Jo 2:14-16</reference>), are what he is here warned against: though the Spirit probably intended the warning to include both in its application to the Church in general.<div eID="gen37689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37690" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also--</hi>Greek, "But"; in contrast to "every good work," <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.21">2Ti 2:21</reference>.<div eID="gen37690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37691" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">youthful--</hi>Timothy was a youth (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Ti 4:12</reference>).<div eID="gen37691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37692" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness--</hi>the opposite of "iniquity," that is, unrighteousness (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Ti 2:19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.11">1Ti 6:11</reference>).<div eID="gen37692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37693" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">peace, with, &c.--</hi>rather, put no comma, "peace with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5">1Ti 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.5">Ep 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.22">Col 3:22</reference>). We are to love all men, but it is not possible to be at peace with all men, for this needs community of purpose and opinion; they alone who call on the Lord sincerely (as contrasted with the false teachers who had only the form of godliness, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.5">2Ti 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>) have this community [Theodoret]. (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.18">Ro 12:18</reference>). <div eID="gen37693" type="x-p"/>
entries.26e7a52cc4ec88c790acc7bc9cf6ef310acd656b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18208"/><div sID="gen37694" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18208"/>23. (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.9">Tit 3:9</reference>.)<div eID="gen37694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37695" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unlearned--</hi>Greek, "undisciplined"; not tending to promote the discipline of faith and morals (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.23">Pr 5:23</reference>). "Uninstructive"; in contrast with "instructing" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.25">2Ti 2:25</reference>), and "wise unto salvation" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.15">2Ti 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen37695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37696" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">avoid--</hi>"decline." <div eID="gen37696" type="x-p"/>
entries.deeed3e0cffd67dfb695701999ad5c668237bcc3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18209"/><div sID="gen37697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18209"/><hi type="bold">24. not strive--</hi>"The servant of the Lord" must imitate his master in not striving contentiously, though uncompromising in earnestly contending for the faith (Jude 3; <reference osisRef="Matt.12.19">Mt 12:19</reference>).<div eID="gen37697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gentle unto all men--</hi>"patient" (Greek, "patient in bearing wrongs") in respect to adversaries. He is to be gentle so that he may occasion no evils; patient so that he may endure evils.<div eID="gen37698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37699" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">apt to teach--</hi>implying not only solid teaching and ease in teaching, but patience and assiduity in it [Bengel]. <div eID="gen37699" type="x-p"/>
entries.62d348529ba8feb911562114289a0f6597975287: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18210"/><div sID="gen37700" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18210"/><hi type="bold">25. instructing--</hi>Greek, "disciplining," instructing with correction, which those who deal in "uninstructive" or "undisciplined questions" need (see on <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.23">2Ti 2:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.20">1Ti 1:20</reference>).<div eID="gen37700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">those that oppose themselves--</hi>Greek, "oppositely affected"; those of a different opinion.<div eID="gen37701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37702" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if ... peradventure--</hi>Greek, "if at any time."<div eID="gen37702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37703" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">repentance--</hi>which they need as antecedent to the full knowledge (so the Greek for 'acknowledgment') of the truth" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">1Ti 2:4</reference>), their minds being corrupted (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.8">2Ti 3:8</reference>), and their lives immoral. The cause of the spiritual ignorance which prompts such "questions" is moral, having its seat in the will, not in the intellect (<reference osisRef="John.7.17">Joh 7:17</reference>). Therefore repentance is their first need. That, not man, but God alone can "give" (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.31">Ac 5:31</reference>). <div eID="gen37703" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d94d06f6020ccaabc93e7c32954d2fc4a408517: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18211"/><div sID="gen37704" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18211"/><hi type="bold">26. recover themselves--</hi>Greek, "awake to soberness," namely from the spiritual intoxication whereby they have fallen into the snare of the devil.<div eID="gen37704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the snare--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.6.11">Ep 6:11</reference>, "the wiles of the devil": <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.7">1Ti 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.9">6:9</reference>).<div eID="gen37705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taken captive by him at his will--</hi>so as to follow the will of "THAT" (the Greek emphatically marks Satan thus) foe. However, different Greek pronouns stand for "him" and "his"; and the Greek for "taken captive" means not "captured for destruction," but "for being saved alive," as in <reference osisRef="Luke.5.10">Lu 5:10</reference>, "Thou shalt catch men to save them unto life"; also there is no article before the Greek participle, which the English Version "who are taken captive," would require. Therefore, translate, "That they may awake ... taken as saved (and willing) captives by him (the servant of the Lord, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24">2Ti 2:24</reference>), so as to follow the will of HIM (the Lord, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24">2Ti 2:24</reference>, or "God," <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.25">2Ti 2:25</reference>)." There are here two evils, the "snare" and sleep, from which they are delivered: and two goods to which they are translated, awaking and deliverance. Instead of Satan's thrall comes the free and willing captivity of obedience to Christ (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.5">2Co 10:5</reference>). It is God who goes before, giving repentance (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.25">2Ti 2:25</reference>); then the work of His servant following is sure to be crowned with success, leading the convert henceforth to "live to the will of God" (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.14">Ac 22:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.2">1Pe 4:2</reference>). <chapter eID="2Tim.2"/>

entries.f341a8e6eed62d76cacbdd355957a1e5f5dd9371: <div eID="gen52019" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen52020" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen52021" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen52021" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen52020" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen52022" type="x-p"/> He exhorts Timothy to constancy, fidelity, and courage; and to acquit himself as a true soldier of Jesus Christ; and patiently expect the fruit of his labors, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.1-2Tim.2.7">2Tim 2:1-7</reference>. What the apostle's doctrine was relative to Christ, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.8">2Tim 2:8</reference>. He mentions his own sufferings and consolations, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.9-2Tim.2.13">2Tim 2:9-13</reference>. What Timothy is to preach, how he is to acquit himself, and what he is to shun, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.14-2Tim.2.16">2Tim 2:14-16</reference>. Of Hymeneus and Philetus, and their errors, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.17">2Tim 2:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Tim 2:18</reference>. Of the foundation of God, and its security, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Tim 2:19</reference>. The simile of a great house and its utensils, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.20">2Tim 2:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.21">2Tim 2:21</reference>. Timothy is to avoid youthful lusts, and foolish and unlearned questions, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.22">2Tim 2:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.23">2Tim 2:23</reference>. How he is to act in reference to false teachers, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24-2Tim.2.26">2Tim 2:24-26</reference>. <div eID="gen52022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52023" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen52023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52024" type="x-p"/> Be strong in the grace - Though the genuine import of the word grace is favor, yet it often implies an active principle communicated from God; light directing how to act, and power enabling to act according to the light.
